questions.passage:
Two drivers leave the same party equally drunk, and each drives home at the same reckless speed. One reaches his front door without incident. The other, at the same moment, meets a child who has stepped off the kerb, and kills her. Most of us judge the second driver far more harshly, and the law will punish him far more severely. Yet the only difference between the two seems to be something over which neither had any control: whether a child happened to be in the road. The example is not fanciful, since traffic law in most countries draws exactly this distinction. It is the problem of moral luck, a phrase that Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel made famous in a pair of essays published in 1976 and 1979. It is a problem because two ideas that we find plausible collide, and neither can be abandoned without cost.

The first idea is the control principle, most closely associated with Kant: people are morally assessable only for what lies within their control. A person cannot deserve blame for being born with a weak constitution, or praise for being born with a gift, and it seems equally unfair to praise or blame anyone for a consequence that no effort of his could have secured or prevented. The second idea is our ordinary practice of assessing people by what they actually do. We judge the surgeon whose patient dies of an unforeseeable complication differently from the one who was careless, but we also judge the careless surgeon whose patient survives differently from the careless surgeon whose patient dies. An assassin whose bullet misses is guilty of attempted murder; one whose bullet strikes is guilty of murder. Our practice appears to treat results as part of what a person has done.

Nagel distinguished four varieties of luck. Resultant luck concerns how things turn out, as with the two drivers. Circumstantial luck concerns the situations in which one happens to be tested: a person who lived under a brutal regime and became complicit might, in a freer country, have lived and died blameless, while those who emigrated before the test arrived were never examined at all. Constitutive luck concerns the temperament and character one is born with, and causal luck concerns the way one’s actions are determined by antecedent circumstances. The argument has the character of a slippery slope. Once the control principle has disposed of resultant luck, it seems to apply with equal force to the others, and as it moves from outcomes to circumstances to character, there is less and less left for which anyone can be held responsible. If what we do is traceable to what we are, and what we are is traceable to what we did not control, then the principle threatens to dissolve the very notion of responsibility it was meant to protect.

One response is to deny that luck should matter: the two drivers are equally blameworthy, and our harsher judgement of the second is a lapse of rationality that a reflective person should correct. The difficulty is that law and common morality persist in treating outcomes as relevant. Attempted murder is punished less than murder, and a reckless driver who kills is punished more than one who does not. Defenders of the practice say that the law responds to harm done, that victims are owed acknowledgement of their loss, and that a legal system indifferent to results would lose the public’s confidence. These are arguments about what institutions need, however, and they do not show that the second driver is more blameworthy; they show only that it may be sensible to treat him as if he were.

Williams took a different route and accepted the role of luck, arguing that it shapes how we rightly feel about ourselves. A lorry driver who, through no fault of his own, runs over a child will feel a regret that differs in kind from that of a bystander, and we would think less of him if he did not. Williams called this agent-regret. It is not guilt, since it does not presuppose blame, but it recognises that being the person who caused the harm is morally significant even when one is not at fault. A third strategy distinguishes between kinds of assessment. Blame may follow choice alone, so that the drivers are equally culpable, while liability follows outcome, so that the driver who kills owes compensation and apology that the other does not. On this view the control principle governs blame and the ordinary practice governs liability, and the apparent collision disappears. Critics reply that the proposal dismisses rather than explains the lingering conviction that the second driver is somehow worse, and that a choice-based account of blame is vulnerable to the very luck in how choices are formed that Nagel called constitutive.

The issue is not merely academic. Psychologists have documented an outcome bias: people judge the quality of a decision by how it turned out, even when told that the outcome was largely a matter of chance. A general who takes a risk and wins is hailed, while one who takes the same risk and loses is condemned. Organisations that punish bad outcomes regardless of the soundness of the decision will find that their staff avoid sensible risks, and the cost of that caution is rarely recorded anywhere. This suggests that decisions should be evaluated by the process that produced them, not merely by results. But the lesson cannot be pushed to the limit, because outcomes are evidence about decision quality. A single death may be bad luck; a surgeon with a long record of deaths is not merely unlucky, and an organisation that ignores such a record in the name of fairness to process has misunderstood the point.

What moral luck reveals is that responsibility is not a single concept but a cluster of practices: blame for choices, liability for outcomes, and the regret of agents for what they have done. The puzzle arises when one principle is asked to govern all of them. The control principle is attractive and, if pushed hard, self-destructive; the practice of judging by results is entrenched and, if pushed hard, unjust. The sensible course may be not to eliminate luck from moral life, which is probably impossible, but to limit the places in which it is allowed to matter, and to be clear, in each case, which of the practices is in play.
questions.question: The author introduces Nagel’s four varieties of luck in order to show that:
options: A) resultant luck is the only variety that is truly beyond the agent’s control, so the other three can safely be ignored in law
B) Nagel believed that the drivers were equally blameworthy, and that the law was therefore mistaken to punish the second more
C) as luck is traced from outcomes to character, the control principle threatens to dissolve responsibility altogether
D) circumstantial luck explains why most people who lived under brutal regimes were less blameworthy than outsiders have supposed
questions.explanation: Explanation: Paragraph 3: the argument is a slippery slope; once the control principle disposes of resultant luck it applies to circumstances and character, leaving little for which anyone can be held responsible. The passage does not rank the varieties by controllability, attribute the drivers’ equality to Nagel, or generalise about people under brutal regimes.

questions.question: Which of the following would be most consistent with Williams’s notion of agent-regret?
options: A) A driver who through no fault kills a child feels a regret that a bystander lacks, and we would think less of him without it.
B) A driver who kills a child through reckless driving feels guilt and accepts that he deserves to be punished by the court for the death.
C) A bystander who witnesses a fatal accident feels the same regret as the driver, since neither was at fault for the death.
D) A driver who kills a child through no fault of his own feels nothing, because he has no responsibility of any kind.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Paragraph 5: agent-regret is felt by the person who caused harm without being at fault; it differs in kind from a bystander’s regret and is not guilt. The other options describe guilt, equal regret, or no regret.

questions.question: The author’s discussion of attempted and completed crimes implies that:
options: A) the law is irrational, since it punishes attempted murder less severely than murder although the two are morally identical in every respect
B) attempted murder is not a crime, because the assassin whose bullet misses has caused no harm to any victim whatsoever
C) the control principle is endorsed by legal systems, which punish only the choices that people make and never their consequences

The passage does not call the law irrational, deny that attempts are crimes, or say law ignores consequences.

Within India, states differ sharply: those that reduced fertility early and invested in schooling and health, such as Kerala and Tamil Nadu, are ageing sooner but have more skilled workers, whereas several northern states will add young workers for decades with weaker schooling and health systems. The same demographic fact can thus yield opposite outcomes according to the institutions and policies that surround it.

At the other end of the transition lies a different problem. Fertility has fallen below the replacement level of about 2.1 births per woman in a growing number of countries, including China, Japan, most of Europe and South Korea, where it is now below one child per woman. India’s fertility has itself fallen to about the replacement level. When births remain below replacement for decades, the population ages and eventually shrinks. Smaller cohorts of workers must support larger cohorts of retirees, pension systems come under strain, and demand for health care rises. Governments have responded with cash payments, tax breaks, housing subsidies and extended parental leave. The effects have been modest. Many studies find that such incentives raise births for a few years and then fade, suggesting that they mainly change the timing of births rather than the number of children women have over their lives.

Why does fertility fall even where wealth and policy could support larger families? Several explanations compete. The opportunity cost of children rises as women’s wages and career prospects improve, especially where the burden of childcare falls on women. Parents in competitive societies invest heavily in each child’s education, which makes each child more expensive and reduces the number they can afford. Housing costs, delayed marriage and changing norms about family size play a part. Across countries, fertility once fell steadily with rising income; among the richest countries, a pattern emerged in which those with better childcare and more equal sharing of domestic work, such as those of northern Europe, had higher fertility than those without. That relationship has since weakened, as fertility has fallen in the Nordic countries too. No single lever has proved reliable, and an explanation that works in one decade may fail in the next.

Responses to an ageing population carry their own politics. Raising the retirement age provokes protests from those who will work longer. Immigration can replenish the workforce but is contested in many of the countries that need it most. Automation may raise output per worker but also reduces the demand for labour, which complicates the view that fewer workers are a disaster; a smaller workforce with better tools and skills can produce as much as a larger one. It also matters what is being measured. The burden of ageing is often summarised by a dependency ratio, the number of people of working age relative to the number of old people. But the economic burden depends less on this demographic ratio than on the number of people actually in work relative to those who are not. A country in which women and older people have high employment rates can support a given age structure far better than one in which they do not.

Demography, it is sometimes said, is destiny. The saying is too strong. Population projections are among the most reliable forecasts available, since those who will be thirty in 2056 have already been born, and the age structure of a country is a fairly firm constraint on what is possible. But constraints define a menu, not a meal. The same age structure can be a dividend or a burden according to whether jobs, skills and institutions are in place, and the same fall in fertility can be managed or can become a crisis. The fertility assumptions behind long-range projections are, in contrast, fragile. Planners are wise to treat the current age structure as a known constraint and the future of fertility as a deep uncertainty.
questions.question: The author’s discussion of fertility in rich countries suggests that:
options: A) countries with generous childcare and equal sharing of domestic work will always have higher fertility than countries without them
B) rising wages for women are the sole cause of falling fertility, and no other factor has had any influence on family size
C) the link between income and fertility has not been stable, so no single policy can be relied on to raise births
D) fertility has stopped falling in the Nordic countries, which demonstrates that the decline in birth rates can be reversed
questions.explanation: Explanation: Paragraph 5: the pattern linking childcare and equality to higher fertility ‘has since weakened’, and ‘no single lever has proved reliable’. The other options turn this into ‘always’, ‘sole cause’, or a claim opposite to the passage (fertility has fallen in the Nordic countries too).

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the author’s final claim?
options: A) Age structure is a fairly reliable constraint, but outcomes depend on jobs, skills and institutions
B) Demography is destiny, since projections of population are reliable and a country’s age structure determines its economic future
C) Fertility projections are so unreliable that planners should disregard demographic forecasts of any kind in framing policy
D) Governments can control fertility through incentives, so ageing populations are a problem that policy can readily eliminate
questions.explanation: Explanation: Paragraph 7: ‘constraints define a menu, not a meal’; age structure is firm but outcomes depend on jobs, skills and institutions; fertility assumptions are fragile. The alternatives endorse determinism, dismiss all forecasts, or overstate the power of incentives.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. A failure of this seasonal pattern can therefore devastate harvests that depend on it.
2. In summer the land heats faster than the sea, so warm air rises and draws in moist air from the ocean.
3. The Indian monsoon is driven by the contrast in temperature between the land and the surrounding ocean.
4. This moist air cools as it rises over land and mountains, and falls as rain.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 3 states the cause in general terms, 2 explains the mechanism, 4 (‘this moist air’) continues the chain to rainfall, and 1 (‘therefore’) draws the consequence.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. Organisations can counter it by asking, at each stage, whether they would begin the project afresh today.
2. This tendency, known as the sunk cost fallacy, turns past losses into a reason for risking further ones.
3. Economists advise that past expenditure that cannot be recovered should not influence present decisions.
4. Yet people often continue a failing project precisely because they have already invested so much in it.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 3 states the advice, 4 (‘Yet’) the contrary behaviour, 2 (‘this tendency’) names it, and 1 (‘it’) offers the remedy.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. A free translation reads smoothly but may lose the flavour of the original.
2. A literal translation, by contrast, preserves the vocabulary and structure but may sound lifeless in the new language.
3. Most good translators therefore steer between the two, deciding case by case what must be kept and what may be sacrificed.
4. Translators face a choice between fidelity to the words of the original and fidelity to its effect on the reader.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 4 sets up the choice, 1 describes one option, 2 (‘by contrast’) the other, and 3 (‘therefore… the two’) concludes.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. Operators therefore fire small thrusters from time to time to restore their altitude.
2. Left alone, this drag would slowly bring them down.
3. Satellites in low orbit travel at tremendous speeds and are subject to constant, small drag from the thin upper atmosphere.
4. The fuel carried for these manoeuvres, rather than any fault in the hardware, usually determines how long a satellite remains useful.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 3 introduces satellites and drag, 2 (‘this drag’) the consequence, 1 (‘therefore’) the remedy, and 4 (‘these manoeuvres’) the limit that results.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. Building more roads is a common response to traffic congestion.
2. Economists call this induced demand, because the supply of road space itself generates the demand that fills it.
3. Pricing road use, rather than expanding it, is therefore often proposed as a more durable remedy.
4. Yet new capacity tends to attract additional traffic until congestion returns to its former level.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 1 states the common response, 4 (‘Yet’) the problem, 2 (‘this induced demand’) names it, and 3 (‘therefore’) gives the proposed alternative.

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'In 1865 William Stanley Jevons observed that more efficient steam engines, rather than reducing coal consumption, increased it, because efficiency made coal-powered activities cheaper and so more widespread. The same logic appears in modern debates: efficient lighting or cars can lead to greater use, offsetting part of the savings, a phenomenon economists call the rebound effect. How large the rebound is varies; in most studies it is partial, not total.'
options: A) Jevons proved that efficiency improvements always increase total resource consumption, so efficiency policy is pointless everywhere in the world.
B) Efficiency gains can raise consumption by making a resource cheaper to use, though studies usually find the offset only partial.
C) Steam engines consumed more coal because they were less efficient than the machines they replaced in nineteenth-century industry in Britain.
D) The rebound effect shows that consumers deliberately waste resources whenever efficiency makes those resources cheaper to use at home.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph describes the Jevons paradox and the rebound effect, noting that offsets are usually partial. The other options say ‘always’, reverse the cause (efficiency, not inefficiency), or add deliberate waste.

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'Robin Dunbar proposed that the number of stable relationships a person can maintain is limited by the size of the neocortex, suggesting a figure of about 150. Critics note that the figure is derived from a statistical extrapolation across primates with wide margins of error, and that human groups vary by culture and by what counts as a relationship. The number is better seen as a rough indicator that cognitive capacity limits social networks than as a precise constant.'
options: A) Dunbar demonstrated that every human being can maintain exactly 150 stable relationships, whatever the culture in which they live.
B) The neocortex has no influence on social group size, since critics have shown that the extrapolation across primates is invalid.
C) Human groups never exceed 150 people, because the cognitive limits that Dunbar identified make larger groups impossible.
D) Dunbar’s figure of about 150 is a rough indication that cognitive limits constrain social networks, not a precise constant.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph presents the figure as a rough indicator, with critics’ caveats. The distractors turn it into an exact universal, deny any influence of the neocortex, or claim larger groups are impossible.

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'The Mercator map, designed in 1569 for navigators because it preserves compass bearings, distorts areas, making regions near the poles look far larger than they are; Greenland appears comparable to Africa, though Africa is many times larger. Because the map has been widely used in classrooms, critics argue that it has shaped, without anyone intending it, an exaggerated impression of the importance of high-latitude countries. Defenders reply that no flat map can preserve all properties, and that the choice of projection should depend on purpose.'
options: A) Mercator’s map is simply wrong and should be removed from schools, since it makes Africa appear much smaller than Greenland is.
B) Flat maps can preserve all properties if the cartographer is skilled enough, so Mercator’s distortion was a design error on his part.
C) Mercator’s map suits navigation but distorts areas; critics say this misleads, defenders say projection should fit purpose.
D) Critics have shown that the Mercator map was intentionally designed to exaggerate the importance of the northern countries of Europe.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph reports the map’s purpose, its distortion, the critics’ view and the defenders’ reply. The distractors condemn the map outright, deny the trade-off between properties, or allege intent that the critics do not claim.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

'A messaging app is valuable mainly because other people use it. For this reason, a new rival with better features may still fail to attract users, because ________.'
options: A) no individual gains from switching unless many others switch at the same time
B) users value features more than the number of people who are already using the existing service, so the rival should have succeeded
C) the existing app is always cheaper to run than any new competitor, whatever the number of its users or the features it offers
D) regulators prevent users from moving between services because the number of competing apps in the market must be kept small
questions.explanation: Explanation: With network effects the value of a service depends on how many others use it, so a better but empty service gives nobody a reason to move first. The other options contradict the premise or invent claims about costs and regulation.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

'A drug tested on a few hundred volunteers may fail to reveal side effects that affect one patient in ten thousand. This is why regulators require surveillance after a drug is marketed, since ________.'
options: A) trials are usually conducted dishonestly, so that the side effects of most drugs are concealed from regulators until later
B) rare harms emerge only when the drug is used by many more people than any trial can include
C) drugs that pass trials are certain to be harmless, so that surveillance serves only to reassure doctors and the public at large
D) side effects that affect one patient in ten thousand are too rare to matter, and are therefore ignored in the approval process
questions.explanation: Explanation: A rare harm is unlikely to appear in a small sample but will appear once millions use the drug, so monitoring continues. The other options allege dishonesty, certainty of harmlessness, or that rare harms are ignored, none of which follows.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY SIMILAR in meaning to 'TACITURN':
options: A) Reserved
B) Voluble
C) Gregarious
D) Exuberant
questions.explanation: Explanation: Taciturn means habitually silent or uncommunicative; 'reserved' is closest. The others describe talkative or outgoing people.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY OPPOSITE in meaning to 'OSTENTATIOUS':
options: A) Flamboyant
B) Modest
C) Showy
D) Garish
questions.explanation: Explanation: Ostentatious means designed to impress or attract notice; 'modest' (unassuming) is the antonym.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY SIMILAR in meaning to 'INIMICAL':
options: A) Amicable
B) Benign
C) Hostile
D) Congenial
questions.explanation: Explanation: Inimical means tending to harm or be hostile; 'hostile' is the synonym. The others are opposites.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY OPPOSITE in meaning to 'PROLIX':
options: A) Verbose
B) Rambling
C) Long-winded
D) Concise
questions.explanation: Explanation: Prolix means using too many words; 'concise' is the antonym. The others are synonyms.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY SIMILAR in meaning to 'CAPITULATE':
options: A) Resist
B) Yield
C) Prevail
D) Withstand
questions.explanation: Explanation: Capitulate means to cease resisting and give in; 'yield' matches. The others mean to hold out.

questions.question:
Choose the correct word to fill in the blank:
'The professor’s ________ insistence on trivial details made the seminar tedious.'
options: A) cursory
B) lax
C) pedantic
D) apathetic
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Pedantic' means excessively concerned with minor details, which fits the insistence on trivia. The others suggest carelessness or indifference.

questions.question:
Choose the pair that best fills the blanks:
'Although her manner was ________, her judgements were remarkably ________.'
options: A) modest; unassuming
B) arrogant; overbearing
C) timid; hesitant
D) unassuming; shrewd
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Although' signals contrast between a quiet manner and sharp judgement. The other pairs are synonyms or do not contrast.

questions.question:
Choose the correct idiom meaning:
'To bite the hand that feeds one' means to:
options: A) accept help reluctantly from a rival
B) harm someone who has helped or supported one
C) refuse a gift out of misplaced pride
D) refuse to eat food prepared by an unfriendly host
questions.explanation: Explanation: The idiom describes ingratitude or hostility towards one’s benefactor.

questions.question: Select the sentence in which the word 'CENSURE' is used correctly:
options: A) The committee voted to censure the minister for misleading Parliament.
B) The authorities decided to censure the film’s violent scenes before its release.
C) Officials moved to censure the book’s offensive chapters before it was published.
D) The board will censure the report’s sensitive details before it is released.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Censure' means to criticise formally and severely. Cutting out material is 'censor'; the other sentences confuse the two.

questions.question:
Choose the correct option to fill in the blank:
'A variety of options ________ available to the students.'
options: A) is
B) was
C) has been
D) are
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'A variety of' takes a plural verb because the real subject is 'options'.

questions.question:
Spot the error in the following sentence:
'The Prime Minister, (A) / accompanied by his advisers, (B) / have arrived (C) / in the capital (D).'
options: A) The Prime Minister,
B) accompanied by his advisers,
C) have arrived
D) in the capital
questions.explanation: Explanation: The subject is the singular 'Prime Minister'; the phrase 'accompanied by his advisers' is parenthetical, so the verb should be 'has arrived'.

questions.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence:
options: A) The climate of Shimla is cooler than Delhi.
B) The climate of Shimla is more cooler than that of Delhi.
C) The climate of Shimla is cooler than that of Delhi.
D) The climate of Shimla is cooler than those of Delhi.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A logical comparison needs like with like: climate with climate ('that of Delhi'). 'More cooler' is a double comparative; 'those' disagrees with 'climate'.

questions.question:
Choose the correct option to fill in the blank:
'She ________ working here for ten years by next March.'
options: A) will have been
B) will be
C) has been
D) would have been
questions.explanation: Explanation: A completed duration reached at a future point takes the future perfect continuous: 'will have been working'.

questions.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence:
options: A) He suggested me to apply early.
B) He suggested that I applied early.
C) He suggested me that I apply early.
D) He suggested that I apply early.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Suggest' is followed by a that-clause with the subjunctive (bare infinitive), not by 'me to' or 'me that'.

questions.question:
Spot the error in the sentence:
'Despite of (A) / the heavy rain, (B) / the match (C) / went ahead (D).'
options: A) Despite of
B) the heavy rain,
C) the match
D) went ahead
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Despite' is not followed by 'of' (compare 'in spite of'); the correct form is 'Despite the heavy rain'.

questions.question:
Choose the correct preposition to fill in the blank:
'The decision is contingent ________ the approval of the board.'
options: A) to
B) with
C) on
D) by
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Contingent' takes 'on' (or 'upon').

questions.question: Identify the grammatically INCORRECT sentence:
options: A) Scarcely had he left the office when it started to rain.
B) He is one of those who always arrives late.
C) She, rather than her brothers, is responsible for the damage.
D) The audience was visibly moved by the closing performance.
questions.explanation: Explanation: In 'one of those who...', the relative pronoun 'who' refers to 'those' (plural), so the verb is 'arrive'.
